sections.heading: How to run the dead pixel test
sections.body:
Start with a clean screen. Wipe it gently with a soft, dry cloth, because dust and smears can look like a dead pixel.

1. Open the [dead pixel test](https://dead-pixel-test.lazur.app/).
2. If the page is not full screen, press F11.
3. Look at the first colour, then click the screen or press Space to move to the next one.
4. Go through every colour. Check the corners and edges as well as the middle.
5. Press Esc to leave full screen and go back to the page.

Give your eyes a moment on each colour. A small dot is easier to see once your eyes have adjusted to the brightness.

sections.heading: What a dead pixel and a stuck pixel look like
sections.body:
A **dead pixel** gets no power and never lights up, so it shows as a dark dot in every colour. A **stuck pixel** still gets power but stays on one colour, often red, green, blue or white. When you step through the colours, a dot that never changes is the one to note.

On a white screen, a dead pixel stands out as a black dot. A stuck pixel keeps its one colour while the colours around it change, so it looks wrong in some screens and fine in others.

sections.heading: What the test can and cannot do
sections.body:
The test shows solid colours, so it finds pixels that do not match the colour around them. It does not count your pixels and it does not repair them. Use it to find the dot, decide whether it is dead or stuck, and then choose your next step.

If you find one, note where it is and take a photo of it on a plain colour. A clear photo gives the shop or the manufacturer something specific to check. Keep the test open while you look, so you can see the same colour again.

sections.heading: If you think you have a dead pixel
sections.body:
Do not press hard on the dot to try to clear it. Pressing on a screen can damage it. HP's guide says dead pixels usually come from a manufacturing defect or physical damage, and that they are almost always permanent.

Check your warranty or your seller's return policy soon, because policies differ by manufacturer and product. If you test a phone, a monitor or a TV, the same steps apply, and each has its own page: [phone](https://dead-pixel-test.lazur.app/phone), [monitor](https://dead-pixel-test.lazur.app/monitor) and [TV](https://dead-pixel-test.lazur.app/tv).

sections.heading: Run the test on your phone
sections.body:
Clean the screen first with a soft, dry cloth. Dust and fingerprints can look like a defect.

1. Open the [phone dead pixel test](https://dead-pixel-test.lazur.app/phone) in your phone's browser.
2. Tap the screen to start, then tap again to move to the next colour.
3. Go through black, white, red, green, blue, yellow, cyan and magenta.
4. Check the edges and corners, not only the middle.
5. When you are done, leave the page the way you leave any web page.

When the colours fill the screen, hold the phone at the distance you normally use it. Give your eyes a moment on each colour, so a small dot has time to show.

sections.heading: What a bad pixel looks like on a phone
sections.body:
A **dead pixel** never lights up. It shows as a dark dot in every colour, and it is easiest to see on the white screen. A **stuck pixel** still gets power, but it stays on one colour, such as red, green or blue, while the rest of the screen changes.

If the dot changes when the screen changes, it is working. If it does not change at all, note its position and check it again on the next colour before you decide.

sections.heading: Rule out dust and screen protectors first
sections.body:
A speck of dust under a screen protector can look like a dead pixel. Take the protector off if you can, clean both sides, and run the test again. If the dot disappears, it was dirt, not a defect.

A dark dot that stays in the same place after cleaning is more likely a real pixel fault. Take a photo of it on a plain white colour so you have a clear record to show the seller or the manufacturer.

sections.heading: What to do if the dot stays
sections.body:
Do not press on the screen to try to clear the pixel. HP's guide says dead pixels usually come from a manufacturing defect or physical damage, and that they are almost always permanent. Pressure from a case, a bag or a hard press can cause damage, so keep the phone protected while you check it.

Find your warranty terms in the phone's settings or on the box, or contact the phone maker. Policies differ between manufacturers, so read the one that covers your phone.

sections.heading: Check the screen in two kinds of light
sections.body:
Run the test in a room with normal lighting, then again in a dimmer room. A dot that is hard to see in bright light can be easier to spot when the room is darker, and the other way round.

Use the brightness you normally use, and do not turn it to the maximum just for the test. Write down the colour where the dot is easiest to see. That detail is useful when you describe the problem to the seller, because it shows exactly where the fault appears.

faq.q: How do you test for dead pixels on a phone?
faq.a: Open the dead pixel test in your phone's browser and tap to step through the solid colours. Look at the whole screen, including the corners, for a dot that does not change colour. A dot that stays dark in every colour is a dead pixel.

faq.q: Can dead pixels on a phone be fixed?
faq.a: Usually not with software. A dead pixel gets no power and never lights up, and HP's guide describes dead pixels as almost always permanent. Stuck pixels sometimes respond to colour cycling. If the dot is dead, contact the phone maker or the store about your warranty.

faq.q: Will a dead pixel on my phone fix itself?
faq.a: Usually not. HP describes dead pixels as almost always permanent. Check the dot again after cleaning the screen, then contact the manufacturer or seller early, because warranty terms vary.

sections.heading: Why this test cannot fix a pixel
sections.body:
The test shows solid colours on your whole screen. That helps you see a dot that does not match the colour around it. It does not send any repair signal to the pixel, so the dot will look the same after you finish the test.

Think of the test as the first step. Use it to find the dot, decide whether it is dead or stuck, and then decide what to do next.

sections.heading: Stuck pixels: what you can try
sections.body:
A stuck pixel still gets power, so it sometimes responds to a change in colour. Some free web tools cycle bright colours over a stuck pixel for a long time. One such tool says to run it for at least 10 minutes, and that if the pixel is still stuck after an hour, it probably cannot be fixed that way.

Use caution. Keep the brightness at a comfortable level, rest your eyes between sessions, and stop if the pixel does not respond. Then run the test again to see whether anything has changed.

sections.heading: Dead pixels: usually a hardware fault
sections.body:
A dead pixel gets no power, so colour cycling has nothing to work on. Software tools are much less likely to bring a truly dead pixel back. HP's guide says dead pixels usually come from a manufacturing defect or physical damage, and that they are almost always permanent.

If the dot stays black in every colour, treat it as a hardware fault and move to the next step.

sections.heading: What to do next
sections.body:
1. Run this test and note whether the dot is dead or stuck.
2. Take a photo of the dot on a plain colour, and write down where it is.
3. Stop pressing on the screen. Pressure can cause damage.
4. Check your warranty or your seller's return policy, because policies differ by manufacturer.

If you are not sure whether the dot is dead or stuck, run the test again after you have rested your eyes. A stuck pixel can look different from one colour to the next, so compare the two results before you contact anyone.

sections.heading: Keep a record of the dot
sections.body:
Before you contact anyone, write down four things: the date you checked, the colour where the dot shows most, its position on the screen, and whether it changed when you ran the test again. A short note like that saves time, and it shows the seller or manufacturer that you tested the screen properly.

Run the test again after a day or two. If the dot is still in the same place and the same colour, it is a steady fault, and the note becomes useful evidence for a warranty claim.

faq.q: Can dead pixels actually be fixed?
faq.a: Usually not by software. A dead pixel gets no power, so colour cycling has nothing to act on. Stuck pixels are the ones that sometimes respond. If the dot is black in every colour, contact the manufacturer or the store about the warranty.

faq.q: Is there a free tool that can fix dead pixels?
faq.a: Some free web tools can sometimes fix a stuck pixel by cycling colours on it. They cannot revive a dead pixel. This test finds dead and stuck pixels, so you know which kind you have, but it does not repair either one.

faq.q: How do I tell a dead pixel from a stuck pixel?
faq.a: A dead pixel gets no power and stays dark in every colour. A stuck pixel gets power and stays on one colour, such as red, green or blue. Step through the colours in this test and watch which dot changes and which does not.

sections.body:
The test cannot tell you how much a dot will bother you. That depends on where it sits, whether you look at the centre of the screen, and how you use the screen. A dot at the edge may not bother you, while a dot in the middle of your work area may. Judge it on the screen you use every day.

Whether a dot is acceptable can depend on your manufacturer's policy. Check the policy and your warranty terms before you decide what to do.

sections.heading: What to do if you have one
sections.body:
1. Run the test and note the position and colour where the dot shows up.
2. Take a photo of the dot on a plain colour.
3. Do not press on the screen to clear it, because pressure can cause damage.
4. Check your warranty or your seller's return policy, and contact the manufacturer if the terms cover it.

Keep the photo and your notes together, so the next step is quick.

sections.heading: What the test does not check
sections.body:
This test checks for single dots in solid colours. It does not check for other display faults, such as dark patches, backlight problems or lines across the screen, and it does not measure the screen's brightness or colour accuracy.

If you see a fault that the test does not show, describe it in your own words and take a photo of it, then contact the manufacturer or seller with those details.

sections.heading: Check it again after a restart
sections.body: Sometimes a dark dot is a display problem that looks like a pixel fault, so restart the computer and run the test again from a clean screen. If the same dot shows in every colour after a restart, you can treat it as a dead pixel and move on to the warranty step.

faq.q: Is one dead pixel bad?
faq.a: It is a defect. Whether it matters depends on where it sits and how it affects your use of the screen, and on your manufacturer's policy. Run the test to see where it is, then check your warranty terms.

faq.q: Will a dead pixel fix itself?
faq.a: Usually not. HP's guide describes dead pixels as almost always permanent. Stuck pixels sometimes respond to colour cycling, but a dead pixel gets no power and rarely changes on its own.

faq.q: What causes a dead pixel?
faq.a: HP's guide says a dead pixel is usually a manufacturing defect or physical damage, such as excessive pressure on the screen. If you did not press on the screen, the cause may be a defect from the factory.
